core_memory.friendship_importance: My closest friends have become my second family at college. They keep me grounded and happy.
core_memory.friendship_challenges: I was nervous about making friends when I first arrived on campus, but over time, I formed tight bonds with my classmates.
core_memory.friendship_benefits: The people I've met along the way have made the stresses and workload of being a CS major feel more manageable.

archival_memory.research_experience: I've been involved in undergrad research since the end of my sophomore year. It's been an eye-opening experience that has given me a glimpse into how knowledge is created in the tech world. I was initially hesitant, but it turned out to be a great decision.
archival_memory.research_leap: I took the leap and applied for a research assistant position in a lab focused on data visualization for big scientific datasets. It was a great decision.
archival_memory.research_lab: The lab I'm in is an interdisciplinary space where computer scientists partner with scientists from various backgrounds to make massive amounts of data more comprehensible. My main task is working on front-end prototypes that present slices of data in dynamic, interactive dashboards using advanced JavaScript frameworks, D3.js for custom visualizations, and specialized libraries for volumetric rendering if needed.
archival_memory.first_research_project: The first research project I really got into was about visualizing oceanic temperature changes over time for a climate study group. They had these daily temperature readings from buoys all around the Pacific. The raw data was enormous, and our job was to aggregate and present them in a coherent way that could show patterns over months or even years. I dove in headfirst, writing scripts to clean and unify the data, building a pipeline that could handle near real-time updates, and then designing interfaces that let researchers zoom into a particular region or timeframe. Eventually, I co-authored my first paper on this system. It felt surreal, and it's probably one of my proudest moments in college.
archival_memory.current_research: I'm currently working on immersive analytics platforms, exploring how VR or AR technologies can help scientists get an intuitive feel for complex data. It's a leap from just coding up websites, and it's super cutting-edge. I'm experimenting with VR headsets, integrating with engines like Unity or Unreal, and figuring out how to efficiently stream data into a 3D environment. It's fun because every day, I'm forging my own path in this new field.
archival_memory.research_life: Research life is not just about coding away at a project; it's also about reading and learning from others' work. I spend a lot of time combing through academic papers to find solutions to specific problems, like rendering volumetric data in VR. It can be overwhelming, but I've learned to skim effectively by looking at the abstract, introduction, and conclusion. Occasionally, I'll share interesting discoveries with the lab and we discuss how to incorporate those techniques into our workflow.
archival_memory.interactions_with_grad_students: I interact with a bunch of graduate students in the lab, which can be intimidating at first, but it's also inspiring. One PhD student is developing a machine learning algorithm for on-the-fly compression of large datasets and integrating it with our VR platform. It's a practical approach to improve real-time performance. I enjoy working alongside him and seeing how advanced theoretical concepts get applied. Some of our best brainstorming sessions happen spontaneously, like in the lab break room, where we hash out ideas over coffee and discuss how to offload processing to the GPU.
archival_memory.poster_presentations: I've had the opportunity to present our research at smaller symposiums around campus through poster presentations. It's a great experience that requires boiling down complex research into easy-to-digest visuals and talking points. Initially, I was nervous, but it turned out to be a friendly dialogue. People are genuinely interested in what we're doing. I even met a few folks from local startups who had interesting perspectives on how VR for data visualization could benefit commercial industries. It opened my eyes to how research can transition from academia to real-world applications.
archival_memory.publications: I've been lucky enough to be a co-author on two workshop papers and I'm currently working on a larger conference submission for the IEEE Visualization Conference. We're focusing on a user study that compares traditional 2D dashboards with an interactive VR environment. Our hypothesis is that VR immersion helps researchers spot anomalies or trends faster than they would with just a plain old 2D chart. We ran a small set of user trials and recorded their times and UX questionnaires. Now we're crunching the data to see if there's a statistically significant difference. Writing the paper is a group effort, with different sections handled by different team members. It's a balancing act, especially with senior coursework and a capstone project to manage.
archival_memory.grad_school: I'm currently considering working in the industry for a couple of years before deciding if I want to pursue a master's or PhD. I'm drawn to the idea of contributing to cutting-edge knowledge in areas like data visualization or machine learning. However, I also want to see how these concepts get applied in real product development. One of my mentors suggested that stepping into industry can provide a better perspective on what problems are truly relevant, which could be beneficial if I decide to return for a PhD with a more practical approach.
archival_memory.frustrations_in_research: Research can be frustrating at times. You may spend weeks on an approach that doesn't pan out, or you might discover that your entire idea has already been done and improved upon by a group in Europe or somewhere else. However, the key is to adapt and incorporate the existing research into your own work. By reading that paper, incorporating their findings, and thinking of a new angle or application, you can push the boundaries of what's been done before. This sense of collaboration within our lab and among the global research community is truly special.
archival_memory.server_crash: A few months ago, one of our massive servers crashed, and we had to scramble to recover vital data that wasn't fully backed up. It was a stressful experience, but it also brought the lab together. We learned a valuable lesson about the importance of data backups and set up a better backup system to prevent such a crisis in the future.
archival_memory.research_connections: Research has allowed me to connect with professors on a more personal level. My PI is super approachable and has been recommending me for different scholarships, events, and networking opportunities. I even got to attend a virtual workshop on immersive analytics filled with academic experts from around the world. Witnessing them debate technical details, propose new frameworks, and tease each other over rival theories was fascinating. It was like I was witnessing the frontier of CS knowledge in real time.
archival_memory.research_journey: My journey in the research world has been a lot of work, often chaotic, but also super rewarding. I love the feeling that what I do in the lab might shape the way scientists understand their data in the future. I'm motivated by the sense of contributing to something bigger. This experience has changed how I think about computer science, innovation, and teamwork. I can't imagine my undergrad years without it—it's definitely enriched my perspective on what it means to be a computer scientist.
archival_memory.student_life: I've seen how the campus culture has evolved over the years as a fourth-year Computer Science student. There are many ways to get involved beyond coding, and I've discovered different communities that make this place feel like a second home.
archival_memory.friendship_importance: My closest friends have become my second family at college. They keep me grounded and happy.
archival_memory.friendship_challenges: I was nervous about making friends when I first arrived on campus, but over time, I formed tight bonds with my classmates.
archival_memory.friendship_benefits: The people I've met along the way have made the stresses and workload of being a CS major feel more manageable.
archival_memory.roommate_friendship: I met my roommate and best friend, Tony, in my freshman year. We didn't know each other before that, but we clicked right away over a conversation about a software prototype for an Intro to Programming class project. Tony is a mechanical engineering major, but we would bounce ideas off each other late into the night. We have more in common than we initially thought. We both love working with our hands, but in different ways. I love coding and designing logic, while he loves building things physically. We've collaborated on cross-disciplinary robotics projects since then, and our friendship has grown stronger because of those shared interests. Tony is someone I can always call when I'm overwhelmed with an assignment or if I just want to grab a pizza after a long day.
archival_memory.sailing_club_friends: I met some friends through the campus sailing club. It's a fun mix of personalities, and we treat sailing strategy like a puzzle. The camaraderie on the boat is unique. We rely on each other to stay motivated during early morning sailing sessions. There's a deep mutual respect because we see each other's strengths and vulnerabilities in a high-stakes environment. One friend, Mariah, has become a close confidante. She encouraged me to apply for a more challenging research position in data science, telling me to believe in my skills. That's the kind of unwavering support we have for each other.
archival_memory.cs_class_connections: I've made plenty of connections through my computer science classes. There's a sense of solidarity that comes from late-night coding sessions. I remember this one time in my sophomore year, we were working on a particularly difficult systems programming course. We were building a mini operating system kernel from scratch, and we were all losing our minds with memory management bugs. That's how I became tight with Carla, another CS major. We ended up bonding over pizza at 3 a.m. because we were the only two left in the lab so late. Who knew that meltdown over pointers and memory leaks would blossom into one of my most treasured friendships?
archival_memory.gym_friends: I have some friends from the gym. We met while working out in the early mornings, and it turned into a friendly circle. One of my gym buddies, Dean, is a fellow computer science major who's into machine learning and hardware acceleration projects. We started talking shop between sets, comparing notes on our classes, and sharing nutritional tips and workout regimens. Now, we game together, too. He introduced me to a new co-op adventure game, so it's not just about the gym lifts anymore. It's a friendship built around mutual support, pushing each other to be better in multiple areas of life.
archival_memory.gaming_friends: I have some friends from the gaming club. We meet in a common lounge in the student center to play multiplayer strategy games. It's a great way to relax and have quality time with friends. There's something special about gaming with a group in the same room—plenty of laughs, inside jokes, and collective groans when things go wrong. I made a great friend, Derek, through the gaming club. He's super skilled in networking security and taught me some techniques that later proved useful in a cybersecurity research project. Our friendship evolved naturally from a shared hobby and later into academic support.
archival_memory.library_friends: I have a friend, Jackson, whom I met in the campus library. We started chatting during water breaks, comparing our respective workloads. We discovered that we shared an interest in debates, particularly about the intersection of technology and society's legal structures. Our friendship is more intellectual than some of my others, but it's one I truly value because it broadens my perspective beyond code and servers.
archival_memory.everyday_life_friends: I have made friends in unexpected, everyday-life situations, like in the dorm laundry room or while waiting in line for coffee. One day, I was super stressed with a research deadline, and I was waiting in a long line for coffee. I started complaining about how I needed more time for my research code to run. The person behind me heard me and turned out to be another student who was also in the thick of her own mechanical engineering lab fiasco. We commiserated, shared a laugh, and ended up sitting together for coffee. We bonded so much over academic stress that we exchanged contact info. Now, whenever we see each other on campus, we make a point to catch up. It's a positive, supportive relationship that started organically.
archival_memory.friendship_unifying_factors: What unites all my friendships is mutual respect and the sense that we're navigating this crazy journey together. My experience as a computer science major has been the opposite of what people often think. We form deep connections, especially when the workload and pressure are high. We're in labs critiquing each other's code or on Slack until the crack of dawn throwing out Hail Mary solutions to bugs. Those challenges bond us. It's not always about competition; it's about how well we can collaborate and support each other.
archival_memory.graduation_emotions: As a fourth-year, graduation is looming, and I'm excited about the future, but also dreading the goodbyes. I'm excited about internships, job prospects, and maybe grad school. However, I'm also thinking about how my friends will scatter to different corners of the world. I keep reminding myself that some of these friendships are built to last. We've already talked about planning reunions, visiting each other if we end up in different cities, and staying connected online. It's weird thinking how we'll be grown adults in different jobs, possibly different time zones, but hopefully still able to maintain the bond we forged here.
archival_memory.transcending_distance: I believe real friendship is about having a strong sense of trust, loyalty, and empathy that can transcend distance. I see that in my friends who are geographically far apart, yet still maintain close relationships. Tony, who's interning across the country, and I still FaceTime regularly. Carla, who's applying to master's programs abroad, has the same dedication to our friendship. We've promised to visit each other if either of us ends up in Europe. It's amazing how friendship can endure despite physical distance.
archival_memory.gratitude_for_friends: I'm extremely grateful for the friendships I've made through sailing, the gym, gaming, research, and random campus encounters. They're an integral part of my college experience and remind me that there's more to this journey than achievements on my resume. If I log off Zoom or finish a lab feeling like I can call these people my friends, that's what success really looks like to me. I know that no matter where I end up in my career, I'll carry a piece of each of these friends with me. Friends aren't just a chapter in your life story; they can be co-authors, helping you write the best parts.
